blocks.text: At 03:00 a first-time mother at 40 weeks phones the maternity unit: her contractions are coming every six minutes and she asks, 'Am I in labour yet?' The honest answer depends on what her cervix is doing, how long this has been going on and how quickly her baby's head is moving down. Labour is not one event but a sequence of mechanical stages, each with its own landmarks.

blocks.markdown: Labour is the process by which regular uterine contractions progressively efface and dilate the cervix and expel the fetus, placenta and membranes. It is divided into **stages**. The **first stage** runs from the onset of regular painful contractions to full cervical dilatation (10 cm) and has two phases: the **latent phase** (irregular contractions with slow cervical change) and the **active phase**, defined by NICE as regular contractions with dilatation from 4 cm. The **second stage** runs from full dilatation to delivery of the baby, with a passive phase (full dilatation, no urge to push) and an active phase (pushing). The **third stage** runs from delivery of the baby to delivery of the placenta and membranes. Some texts add a **fourth stage** for the first hour or two after birth, in which the risk of postpartum bleeding is highest.

rows: Nulliparous: average about 8 hours, unlikely over 18 hours; parous: about 5 hours, unlikely over 12 hours
Nulliparous: birth usually within 3 hours of active second stage; parous: within 2 hours
Physiological up to 60 minutes; active management usually within 30 minutes
blocks.caption: Stages of labour.

blocks.title: Engagement and station
blocks.text: A fetal head is engaged when its widest presenting diameter (the biparietal diameter) has passed through the pelvic inlet; clinically, no more than two-fifths of the head are palpable above the pelvic brim on abdominal examination. Station is the position of the leading bony part relative to the ischial spines: station 0 is at the spines.

blocks.markdown: **Cardinal movements of labour.** The fetal head must pass through a pelvis whose widest diameter changes from transverse at the inlet to anteroposterior at the outlet. In the commonest presentation, vertex occipito-anterior (OA), the head makes a series of movements: **engagement** (usually occipito-transverse), **descent**, **flexion** (the chin tucks, presenting the smallest diameter, the suboccipitobregmatic of about 9.5 cm), **internal rotation** (the occiput rotates anteriorly under the pubic symphysis so that the sagittal suture lies in the anteroposterior diameter of the outlet), **extension** (the head pivots under the symphysis and is born), **restitution** (the head untwists to realign with the shoulders) and **external rotation** (the shoulders rotate to the anteroposterior diameter, seen as the head turning), followed by **expulsion** (the anterior then posterior shoulder deliver, then the body).

blocks.title: Tracing the cardinal movements
blocks.prompt: At full dilatation a midwife finds the head at station +1 with the sagittal suture in the transverse diameter and the posterior fontanelle to the maternal left. Describe the next movements in order until the baby's head is born.

steps.text: The head is in the occipito-transverse position at the mid-pelvis; the outlet is widest anteroposteriorly, so it must rotate. This is internal rotation of the occiput 90 degrees anteriorly, bringing the sagittal suture into the anteroposterior diameter.

As the head reaches the perineum, uterine force and the pelvic floor direct the head upward and forward: extension. The occiput passes under the pubic arch and the head is born as the vertex, forehead, face and chin deliver.

After birth of the head, the head untwists to realign with the shoulders (restitution) and then turns further as the shoulders rotate into the anteroposterior diameter (external rotation); the anterior shoulder is delivered, then the posterior.

blocks.answer: Internal rotation, extension, restitution, external rotation and then expulsion of the shoulders and body.

blocks.markdown: **The partogram** is a graph that records the progress of labour and the condition of mother and fetus on one page. The WHO modified partogram begins at the start of the active phase (4 cm). It plots **cervical dilatation against time** with an **alert line** (expected progress of 1 cm per hour) and an **action line** drawn 4 hours to the right of it. It also records the **descent of the head** in fifths palpable abdominally, **contractions** (number in 10 minutes and duration), **fetal heart rate**, **liquor colour**, **moulding**, maternal pulse, blood pressure, temperature, urine and drugs or oxytocin given. A plot to the right of the alert line prompts review; a plot reaching the action line prompts intervention. Newer WHO guidance (the Labour Care Guide) recognises that many normal women progress more slowly than 1 cm per hour at the start of the active phase, so the partogram line must be interpreted with the whole clinical picture.

blocks.title: Plotting against the alert and action lines
blocks.prompt: A woman reaches 4 cm at 09:00. By 13:00 she is 6 cm. The alert line starts at 4 cm at 09:00 and rises 1 cm per hour; the action line is 4 hours to the right. Where is she relative to each line?

steps.text: Expected dilatation at 13:00 on the alert line is 4 cm plus 4 hours at 1 cm per hour.
She is at 6 cm, which is 2 cm behind the alert line, so her plot lies to the right of it.
The action line is 4 hours to the right: it would show 4 cm at 13:00, so at 13:00 she is at 6 cm, to the left of the action line. She has crossed the alert line but not the action line.

blocks.answer: She has crossed the alert line (prompting review and encouragement) but not the action line, so she needs reassessment rather than urgent intervention.

blocks.markdown: **Analgesia in labour.** Pain arises from uterine contractions and cervical dilatation (visceral pain carried by T10 to L1) and later from stretch of the vagina and perineum (somatic pain through the pudendal nerve, S2 to S4). Options range from non-pharmacological to regional anaesthesia. The choice is individual and the woman can change her mind.

rows: Entonox (50 percent nitrous oxide, 50 percent oxygen)
Opioids (for example intramuscular pethidine or diamorphine; teaching examples)
Maternal nausea and sedation, neonatal respiratory depression and feeding effects
Epidural analgesia (local anaesthetic with or without opioid in the epidural space)
Most effective pain relief; can be topped up for operative delivery
Hypotension, motor block, longer second stage and more instrumental births, headache after dural puncture, urinary retention
blocks.caption: Comparing analgesic options.

blocks.title: Checking a local anaesthetic dose
blocks.prompt: An epidural top-up of 10 mL of 0.1 percent bupivacaine is requested. How many milligrams of bupivacaine is this? (Teaching example only.)

steps.text: A 0.1 percent solution contains 0.1 g in 100 mL, that is 100 mg in 100 mL, or 1 mg per mL.

items: First stage: latent then active (4 cm to full); second: full dilatation to birth; third: placenta.
Cardinal movements: engagement, descent, flexion, internal rotation, extension, restitution, external rotation, expulsion.
The partogram plots dilatation against an alert line (1 cm per hour) and an action line 4 hours to its right.
Analgesia: non-pharmacological, Entonox, opioids, epidural, each with different effectiveness and risks.

blocks.title: Pair the mechanism with the anatomy
blocks.text: Rotation, extension and restitution make sense only if you remember that the pelvic inlet is widest from side to side while the outlet is widest from front to back. The head has to rotate to match whichever diameter it is passing through.

points: Labour has three stages (first with latent and active phases, second, third), and the first hour after birth is sometimes called the fourth stage.
The head moves through engagement, descent, flexion, internal rotation, extension, restitution, external rotation and expulsion because of the changing diameters of the pelvis.
The partogram records dilatation against an alert line and action line with descent, contractions, fetal heart rate and maternal observations.
Analgesia options trade effectiveness against side effects: epidural is most effective but lengthens the second stage and increases instrumental birth; opioids risk neonatal respiratory depression.

questions.stem: A woman is examined and the cervix is fully dilated. The baby is not yet born. Which stage of labour is this?

options.text: Latent phase of the first stage
Active phase of the first stage
Second stage
Third stage

distractorRationale.a: The latent phase ends at about 4 cm.
distractorRationale.b: The first stage ends at full dilatation.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: the second stage runs from full dilatation to birth of the baby.
distractorRationale.d: The third stage begins after the baby is born.

questions.explanation: The second stage starts when the cervix is fully dilated and ends with the birth of the baby. The third stage then runs until the placenta and membranes are delivered.

questions.stem: During descent through the mid-pelvis, a fetal head in the occipito-transverse position rotates so that the occiput lies under the pubic symphysis. What is the main reason for this movement?

options.text: The pelvic outlet is widest in the anteroposterior diameter so the sagittal suture aligns with it
The pelvic inlet is widest in the anteroposterior diameter
The cord is wrapped around the neck
The uterus changes shape

questions.correctOptionText: The pelvic outlet is widest in the anteroposterior diameter so the sagittal suture aligns with it

distractorRationale.a: Correct: internal rotation matches the head to the outlet's widest diameter.
distractorRationale.b: The inlet is widest transversely, which is why the head engages transversely.
distractorRationale.c: A nuchal cord does not cause rotation.
distractorRationale.d: Uterine shape does not determine rotation.

questions.explanation: The pelvic inlet is widest from side to side and the outlet widest from front to back. The head therefore engages in the transverse diameter and internally rotates to fit the outlet.

questions.stem: After the fetal head is born, it turns to face the mother's thigh to re-align with the shoulders. What is this movement called?

options.text: Engagement
Flexion
Restitution
Descent

distractorRationale.a: Engagement occurs when the biparietal diameter passes the inlet.
distractorRationale.b: Flexion occurs earlier, presenting a smaller diameter.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: the head untwists to realign with the shoulders; external rotation follows as the shoulders rotate.

questions.explanation: After extension and delivery of the head, the neck untwists so the occiput realigns with the shoulders, a movement called restitution. It is followed by external rotation as the shoulders rotate into the anteroposterior diameter.

questions.stem: On a WHO partogram, a woman's plotted cervical dilatation has reached the action line. Which interpretation and response is most appropriate?

options.text: Progress is normal; continue routine observation
Progress is slow and needs senior review, assessment of the cause and consideration of intervention
The woman is in the second stage
Immediate caesarean section is always mandatory

questions.correctOptionText: Progress is slow and needs senior review, assessment of the cause and consideration of intervention

distractorRationale.a: Reaching the action line is not normal progress.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: the action line signals delay and prompts assessment of powers, passage and passenger.
distractorRationale.c: The second stage starts at full dilatation.
distractorRationale.d: Intervention is individualised and caesarean section is not automatic.

questions.explanation: The action line lies 4 hours to the right of the alert line, so plotting on it indicates significant delay. It triggers a clinical review to identify the cause and decide on amniotomy, oxytocin or operative delivery.

questions.stem: Which statement about epidural analgesia in labour is most accurate?

options.text: It is the most effective form of pain relief but is associated with hypotension and a longer second stage
It causes neonatal respiratory depression more than opioids
It cannot be topped up for caesarean section
It is self-administered by the woman

questions.correctOptionText: It is the most effective form of pain relief but is associated with hypotension and a longer second stage

distractorRationale.b: Systemic opioids, not epidural local anaesthetic, are associated with neonatal respiratory depression.
distractorRationale.c: An in-situ epidural can be topped up for operative delivery.
distractorRationale.d: Entonox is self-administered; epidurals are given by an anaesthetist.

questions.explanation: Epidural analgesia gives the most complete pain relief, but sympathetic block can cause maternal hypotension, motor block can prolong the second stage and instrumental delivery rates increase. It can be topped up for caesarean section.

questions.stem: True or false: Pethidine given intramuscularly shortly before delivery can cause respiratory depression in the newborn.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Opioids cross the placenta and the fetal metabolites persist, so neonatal respiratory depression is possible, especially if given within a few hours of birth. Naloxone can reverse this, and the effect is why opioids are used cautiously late in labour.

questions.stem: On a WHO partogram the alert line expects progress of 1 cm per hour. A woman is 5 cm dilated at 14:00 and her plot starts on the alert line. What cervical dilatation in cm does the alert line predict at 17:30?
questions.explanation: From 14:00 to 17:30 is 3.5 hours, so the line predicts 3.5 cm of progress. Adding this to 5 cm gives 8.5 cm.

questions.stem: An epidural infusion delivers 8 mL per hour of 0.125 percent bupivacaine (teaching example only). How many milligrams of bupivacaine does it deliver in 3 hours?
questions.explanation: A 0.125 percent solution contains 1.25 mg per mL, so 8 mL contains 10 mg per hour. Over 3 hours this is 30 mg.

questions.stem: A woman presents with regular contractions and a cervix 5 cm dilated. Describe the stages of labour she will pass through, and the sequence of movements of the fetal head from engagement to delivery of the shoulders.
markingGuide: First stage from regular contractions to full dilatation with latent and active phases (active from 4 cm)
Second stage from full dilatation to birth, third stage from birth of baby to delivery of placenta and membranes
Internal rotation to occipito-anterior aligned with the anteroposterior outlet
Restitution and external rotation realigning with the shoulders
Link rotation to the changing pelvic diameters (inlet transverse, outlet anteroposterior)
questions.explanation: The fetal head performs a fixed sequence because the pelvis changes shape from inlet to outlet. Describing the movements in order and linking each to its mechanical purpose demonstrates understanding rather than recall.

questions.stem: Compare Entonox, intramuscular opioids and epidural analgesia for pain relief in labour, covering effectiveness, main side effects and a situation in which each might be the best choice.
markingGuide: Entonox: moderate effect, rapid onset and offset, self-administered, nausea and light-headedness; suits a woman wanting short-term relief and control
Opioids: moderate effect, nausea, sedation, delayed gastric emptying, neonatal respiratory depression if given close to delivery; suits a woman in early labour who does not want regional block
Epidural: most effective, can be topped up for instrumental or caesarean birth; hypotension, motor block, longer second stage, more instrumental births, headache, urinary retention
Mention non-pharmacological methods as first-line options
Contraindications to epidural such as coagulopathy, sepsis at the site or refusal
Individual choice and the right to change one's mind
questions.explanation: No single method is superior in every circumstance. The best option depends on the stage of labour, desired degree of pain relief and the woman's preferences, balanced against maternal and neonatal side effects.
